title: Printing press? Big deal!
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore the invention of the printing press, centered on Johannes Gutenberg. They cover earlier precursors: Chinese and Korean woodblock printing, the Diamond Sutra (868 CE), block books in fourteenth-century Europe, Bi Sheng's movable type (around 1041), and Korean metal movable type (1234). They explain why alphabetic movable type suited Gutenberg's language better than Chinese characters, and why water-based ink was a problem that oil-based ink solved. They describe Gutenberg's life, his lawsuits (Strasbourg trinket venture, the lawsuit with investor Johann Fust), the production of the Gutenberg Bible (42-line Bible, around 180 copies), how his casting of metal type and his press worked, and the press's lasting impact on information, literacy, and ideas. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about a sweepstakes win.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to the printing press
segments.summary: Hosts open the show, mention listener-made stingers, and introduce the episode topic of the printing press and Johann Gutenberg, with banter about his name and stamps.

segments.title: Woodblock printing and early block books
segments.summary: Explanation of woodcut printing and European block books in the 1400s. The hosts note that the Chinese printed earlier, citing the Diamond Sutra (868 CE) and carved pages printed in reverse, and mention the Tripitaka Koreana.

segments.title: Early movable type in China and Korea
segments.summary: Bi Sheng's movable type around 1041 CE and Korean experiments with metal type, including Shin Shu-ji's work in 1234. The hosts say these ideas were precursors to Gutenberg's press.

segments.title: Why printing did not take off in Asia
segments.summary: Discussion of why movable type failed to spread in China and Korea: thousands of complex characters versus Gutenberg's twenty-six-letter alphabet, and the difficulty of storing and retrieving characters. The hosts say the Mongols may have spread the idea west, though this is uncertain.

segments.title: Gutenberg's early life and lawsuits
segments.summary: Gutenberg's aristocratic background in Mainz, the scarce records of his early life, and his entrepreneurial, perfectionist character. Court records from lawsuits with creditors and investors, including the Strasbourg trinket venture, shaped what is known about him.

segments.title: Gutenberg's first projects and the Bible
segments.summary: Gutenberg started with smaller printing projects, such as a grammar book and broadsheets, before taking on the Bible. The 42-line Bible had about 1,286 pages over two volumes. Only about 180 copies were printed, and 49 survive today.

segments.title: Johann Fust, the lawsuit, and the Bible's value
segments.summary: Gutenberg borrowed from investor Johann Fust, the project took about two years, and Fust sued after the Bible was completed. The court sided with Fust, who took the presses and plates. The hosts estimate the Bibles' value and debate whether Gutenberg died poor.

segments.title: How the Gutenberg press worked
segments.summary: Process details: punch-cut metal type cast from alloy, filing letters to uniform size, the compositor setting type, oil-based ink, dampened paper, the screw press, red rubrication, and registration pins.

segments.title: Impact of the printing press
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the printing press as the start of the first information age. They say it made copies cheaper and harder to suppress, with effects on the Enlightenment, revolutions, and democracy, citing a History.com article.

segments.title: Listener mail: sweepstakes win
segments.summary: Listener Devin Johns shares a sweepstakes win from Interstate Battery and Firestone, in which he won a truck and sold it to pay off debt. The hosts respond to the sweepstakes episode.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts sign off and give contact information for listener mail.
